desc:
You start with capital coins and want to own at least target coins. There are n projects. Project i can be started only if you currently own at least costs[i] coins; starting it does not use up the coins, and when it finishes you immediately gain profits[i] coins. Each project can be done at most once, one at a time.

Return the fewest projects needed to reach target coins, or -1 if it is impossible. If you already own enough coins, the answer is 0.

target = 10, capital = 2
costs   = [2, 5, 3, 9]
profits = [3, 4, 2, 8]
start project 0 (cost 2)  -> 5 coins
start project 1 (cost 5)  -> 9 coins
start project 3 (cost 9)  -> 17 coins
answer = 3   (no two projects can reach 10)
hints: Try small cases by hand: after doing exactly j projects, what is the largest amount of capital you could have?
Greedy: at every step, among the projects you can afford right now, take the one with the largest profit. Taking a smaller profit never leaves you with more capital or more choices.
Sort the projects by cost. Move every project that has become affordable into a max-heap keyed by profit, pop the best one, and repeat until the capital reaches the target or the heap runs dry.
editorial: Because every profit is positive, owning more coins never hurts, and a project that is affordable stays affordable. Take any plan with j projects; swapping one of its projects for an affordable project of larger profit cannot reduce the capital at any later moment. So the greedy plan (always the most profitable affordable project) maximises the capital after exactly j projects, for every j at once. The answer is therefore the first j at which greedy reaches the target.

Implementation: sort projects by cost; a pointer feeds every project with cost ≤ capital into a max-heap of profits. Pop the largest profit, add it to the capital, count one project, and feed newly affordable projects. If the heap is empty while the target has not been reached, nothing more can be started and the answer is -1.

Sorting costs O(n log n) and each project enters and leaves the heap once, so the total time is O(n log n) and the space is O(n). This is the same engine as the classic “maximise capital with k projects” problem, but asking for the smallest count instead of the best final capital.
solution:
import heapq


def fewestProjects(target, capital, costs, profits):
    order = sorted(range(len(costs)), key=costs.__getitem__)
    heap = []  # negated profits of affordable projects
    j = 0
    count = 0
    while capital < target:
        while j < len(order) and costs[order[j]] <= capital:
            heapq.heappush(heap, -profits[order[j]])
            j += 1
        if not heap:
            return -1
        capital -= heapq.heappop(heap)
        count += 1
    return count
